readerTitle: Plan your week before it plans you
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류창고 운영 매니저, 소프트웨어 회사 분석팀 리더) · 적용 레슨: 시간 관리 + 에너지 관리
insight: 주간 계획은 할 일을 빈칸에 채우는 일이 아니라, 중요한 일을 먼저 놓고 에너지가 높은 시간에 맞춰 배치하는 일이다.
misconception: 빈 시간을 넉넉히 남겨 두면 중요한 일은 알아서 하게 된다. 시간만 확보하면 언제 하든 결과는 같다.

sources.text: PIXO 유닛 PPL-01의 개념 레슨 (PPL-01-03 시간 관리, PPL-01-04 에너지 관리)
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 실제 기업, 연구, 통계를 쓰지 않았습니다. 모든 인물·일정·시간은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 7번 카드의 회의 시간(주 14시간)은 가정입니다.
PPL-01-03, PPL-01-04 개념 레슨의 용어와 정의가 이 레슨의 피드백 문장과 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Plan your week before it plans you
body: It's Monday, 7 a.m. Maya runs operations at a regional distribution warehouse. By 9 a.m., a late truck, two staff calls and a stock question have already filled her morning.
The one project that would fix her biggest problem, pick errors, has been on her list for six weeks. This lesson walks through her week.

image.label: A manager at a warehouse desk with a calendar filling up
image.brief: 물류창고 사무실 책상에 앉은 매니저. 앞에 놓인 주간 캘린더에 작은 메모지(전화, 트럭, 재고 질문)가 빠르게 붙어 빈칸을 덮고, 구석에 'Fix pick routes' 메모 하나만 밀려나 있음. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where does the big project go?
body: Maya wants to redesign the pick routes this week. It needs about three hours of focused thinking. Nothing forces her to do it now, so it keeps slipping.

options.text: Keep the week loose and do it when things calm down
options.feedback: **Managing your time:** urgent work expands to fill open space. Important-but-not-urgent work needs a fixed slot, or it waits forever.

options.text: Book two 90-minute blocks on Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, before the floor walk
options.feedback: This uses both ideas. **Time:** the important work is placed first. **Energy:** it lands when she thinks most clearly.

options.text: Do it after the evening shift, when the building is quiet
options.feedback: It protects the time, but **managing your energy** says tired thinking produces weaker plans. Quiet isn't the same as sharp.

cards.title: Start with outcomes, not tasks.
body: Maya used to plan by listing everything and fitting it in. The urgent items always won.
Now she asks one question on Monday: *what one or two results would make this week a success?* This week, it's the new pick routes and a fair holiday rota.
She puts those on the calendar **first**. Calls, emails and floor problems fill in around them, not the other way round.

cards.title: Match the work to the hour.
body: Next, Maya looks at her own pattern. She's sharp early. After the afternoon floor walk, she's drained.
So she sorts work by the energy it needs. Deep thinking goes in the mornings. Routine work, like approvals and email, goes after lunch. People conversations go where she still has patience.
An hour isn't just an hour. **Where** it sits changes what she gets out of it.

image.label: A weekly grid colored by energy level
image.brief: 월~금 주간 그리드. 오전 칸은 진한 색(High energy)에 'Pick routes', 'Rota', 오후 칸은 연한 색(Low energy)에 'Email', 'Approvals'. 목요일 하루 전체는 회색 'Inventory count'. 단순한 플랫 인포그래픽.

cards.title: Thursday is inventory count.
body: The monthly stock count runs Thursday, 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. Maya also needs a tough call with a supplier who keeps shipping late.
When should she schedule the call?

options.text: Thursday afternoon, right after the count, since she's free
options.feedback: The calendar is free, but she won't be. **Managing your energy:** a hard negotiation needs a fresh mind, not the end of an eight-hour count.

options.text: Wednesday morning, after one of her project blocks
options.feedback: It lands in high-energy time and still before the count. Both **time** and **energy** are working for her.

options.text: Friday morning, after a night's rest
options.feedback: Good for **energy**. But the late shipments keep hurting all week, so waiting costs something too.

cards.title: A full plan is a fragile plan.
body: Maya's plan broke on Tuesday. A forklift went down and ate her first project block.
Two habits keep the plan useful. First, leave some slots open on purpose, so surprises have somewhere to go. Second, treat the plan as a draft. If a block gets lost, move it. Don't delete it.
On Friday, she spends ten minutes looking back. What happened to the blocks? That review is how next week's plan gets better.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a software company.
body: Jon leads a small analytics team at a large software company. He has 14 hours of meetings this week, a revenue forecast model due next Friday, and two new hires who need his help.
How should he plan the week?

options.text: Move or decline a few meetings to free two morning blocks for the model, and meet the new hires in the afternoons
options.feedback: **Time:** the most important work gets fixed slots first. **Energy:** focused work goes where he's sharpest, and the people work still gets real time.

options.text: Work on the model in the 30-minute gaps between meetings
options.feedback: No meeting gets moved, but **managing your time** warns that deep work rarely gets done in small, broken pieces. The deadline arrives with a half-built model.

options.text: Cancel everything, including the new hires' sessions, and spend the whole week on the model
options.feedback: The model gets done, but the new hires stall. And long days of one hard task drain **energy** faster than a mix does.

cards.title: Put the important work first, then put it at your best hours.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Managing your time:** decide the week's one or two key results and book them before anything else. **Managing your energy:** place each task where your energy fits it, and leave room for surprises.
**Try it today:** write down the one result that would make next week a success. Then book two blocks for it in your sharpest hours.
